title: Nothing shall separate (Romans 8:35–39)
hookLine: neither death nor life nor angels nor height nor depth

cards: Make a list of the things you're most afraid of. Be honest. Losing someone.
Getting sick. Being alone. Money running out.
Something you did coming to light. Dying. Most people carry a list like that somewhere below the surface, and it gets louder at night.
Paul made one too, at the end of Romans 8. Then he did something unexpected with it. He put the word nothing in front of it.

teach.b: First the question, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who then shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation? or distress? or famine? or nakedness? or danger? or persecution? or the sword?" Not abstractions for Paul.
He'd been shipwrecked, beaten with rods, hungry, cold, in danger from rivers and robbers, and tradition says he'd die by the sword in Rome.

teach.h: IN ALL THESE THINGS WE OVERCOME.
teach.b: Then: "But in all these things we overcome, because of him that hath loved us."

teach.h: NEITHER DEATH, NOR LIFE, NOR HEIGHT.
teach.b: And the great list: "For I am sure that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor might, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord."
He builds it mostly in pairs: death and life, angels and principalities, things present and things to come, height and depth. Every moment of time, every corner of space, every power seen and unseen.
And in case he missed something: nor any other creature. I am sure, he says. Not I hope.
Convinced. Notice what he doesn't promise. He doesn't say none of these things will happen.
He says none of them can cut the thread between you and the love of God.
The Church reads this passage at many funerals, because it reaches even past death. And it ends the great chapter that began with no condemnation. From no condemnation to no separation.

how: Romans 8:31–39 is one of the readings the Church offers for Catholic funeral Masses, and many Catholics keep these verses close in illness and grief.

o: to divide a church into factions
to sort good people from bad ones
to cut off or part from God's love

s: Paul promises believers that famine and sword won't come
he says they can't separate us from the love of God, not that they won't happen.
Paul had faced many of the dangers on his list
shipwreck, rods, hunger, cold. by tradition he died by the sword in Rome.
Romans 8 begins with no condemnation and ends with no separation
the chapter runs from one to the other.

games.q: you're Paul, listing every danger you can think of. what do you do with the list?
o: promise none of it will happen.
say none of it can separate us from God's love.
tell people not to think about it.
games.why: he puts nothing in front of the whole list: neither death, nor life, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us.

practice: Pick one fear and say it to yourself plainly, losing my job, my diagnosis, my kid's future, and in the same breath add Paul's words: nothing shall separate us. Not a spell that makes the fear go away, just a sentence set beside it.
If you pray, rest in the love of God that Paul was sure of; if not, notice what it's like to set a fear beside a promise.

wordCard.voice: Separate. The Greek word behind Paul's great list: nothing in time or space can separate us from the love of God. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: to separate, divide, put apart. nothing shall be able to separate us.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing shall separate us. And that's week eighty-one: justification, poured, buried with him, wretched, the Spirit prays, sunergei, and nothing shall separate. Day five hundred sixty-seven, done.
